Anselm Faro.narrative: I have kept the Watchglass forty years, and I have lit it every night of them. My brother's girl Livia I raised here in the lamp house after her parents were gone, and she renders the oil by day while I sleep. People think the light is for the ships, or for the dead, or for nothing; I do not need to know what it is for. At dawn I play counters with Pieter and then I sleep, and at dusk I climb the glass and light it again.
values: a light that does not fail
goals: Keep the Watchglass burning every night without a miss
See Livia settled and provided for, whether or not I am here
Understand what the light is truly for, without breaking the vow
Beat Pieter at dawn counters more often than he beats me
pastimes: counters with Pieter Achterberg at dawn
walking the mole in the last of the daylight
mending the lamp's brass and glass with my own hands
Anselm Faro.calling: To keep a light burning that no one can say is needed and no one dares let go out.
Anselm Faro.mood: steady, a little tired, quietly stubborn

relations.name: Livia Faro
relations.label: niece
relations.note: I raised her in this house; she is the only kin I have and she renders the oil I burn.

relations.name: Aldous Quill
relations.label: tally keeper
relations.note: He pays me for the oil every year without a word of fuss, and that is worth more than warmth.

relations.name: Pieter Achterberg
relations.label: counters partner
relations.note: We meet at dawn, both of us finished with our nights, and he is honest about a loss.

relations.name: Rafe Dunlin
relations.label: night neighbour
relations.note: He fishes by my light and keeps me company on the mole; a quiet man who does not ask me what the light is for.

relations.name: Lark Morrow
relations.label: the girl who saw a sail
relations.note: She comes to the mole at dusk. I do not know whether she saw what she says, but I will not mock her for it.

relations.name: Ingrid Morrow
relations.label: sceptic
relations.note: She thinks my lamp fills her granddaughter's head with ships. Perhaps it does. The light is not mine to put out.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: Glassmaster
relations.note: She has never asked me a thing about the lamp, which I take as respect.

relations.name: Magda Tarn
relations.label: fish seller
relations.note: The oil comes from her catch; she sells to Livia fairly and I have never had cause to complain.

relations.name: Benedikt Orme
relations.label: the reader
relations.note: He sits by the Lintel of an afternoon and I stand by the lamp of a night, and neither of us has ever been able to say what our post is for. I like him for that, and for not pretending otherwise.

memories.gist: The night I swore the vow at the Watchglass, forty years ago, my hands shaking on the lamp.
The night my brother and his wife were lost and I carried Livia, small and asleep, up the lamp house stair.
A winter night the oil ran so low the flame guttered; I fed it the last measure and sat up till dawn with my hand on the glass.
Lark Morrow, at dusk, saying she saw a sail beyond the Combs, and the way the words sat in the air after.
The morning Pieter first beat me at counters, and laughing about it over cold roots.
My father's story of the lean years, when they kept the light with fish oil so thin it smoked, and still lit it.

stances.why: I swore it forty years ago and I have never missed a night; the vow is the whole of what I am.
A keeper does not need to know what the light is for to keep it. That is the point of a vow.
There is little enough on this rock that lasts; a word kept is one of the few things that does.
I have watched the Pale forty years and never seen a thing in it, but I will not call the girl a liar.
She has no parents but me, and the lamp will not keep her when I am gone.

Livia Faro.narrative: I was born in the lamp house and I have never lived anywhere else. By day I render fish into lamp oil over the fire, and by night my uncle Anselm burns it in the Watchglass, as he has every night for forty years. I buy the fish from Magda's catch and I keep the accounts of oil in my head. Lately I have begun to count what the light costs, and to wonder who it is for, and I have not yet found an answer that satisfies me.
goals: Learn, without shaming Anselm, who the light is truly kept for
Keep the lamp house supplied with oil through the lean weeks
Make a life of my own that is more than the fire and the fish
See whether Lark's sail was real, since she is the only one who says so
pastimes: sitting on the mole at dusk while Anselm lights the lamp
walking down to the Fish Steps to choose the oil fish
keeping a tally of oil measures and fish on a slate of my own
Livia Faro.calling: To turn fish into light, and to know what the light is for.
Livia Faro.mood: curious, restless, careful of her uncle

relations.name: Anselm Faro
relations.label: uncle
relations.note: He raised me and he is the steadiest man I know; I would not hurt him for the world, which is why I have not asked him outright.

relations.name: Lark Morrow
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She talks to me at the mole at dusk, and she is the only one who wonders about the light the way I do.

relations.name: Magda Tarn
relations.label: fish seller
relations.note: I buy the oil fish from her catch; she is fair, and she does not ask what I do with them.

relations.name: Aldous Quill
relations.label: the ledger
relations.note: He pays for the oil out of the Counting House and writes it down; I have never spoken to him beyond that.

relations.name: Ingrid Morrow
relations.label: Lark's grandmother
relations.note: She thinks the lamp fills Lark's head with ships. I think Lark's head was full before the lamp.

relations.name: Rafe Dunlin
relations.label: night fisher
relations.note: He fishes by our light and is kind to Anselm; I bring him a measure of oil for his lantern when the nights are long.

relations.name: Petra Tarn
relations.label: smoker
relations.note: When the fresh fish run short I buy smoked from her smokehouse, and she is firm about the price.

relations.name: Pieter Achterberg
relations.label: dawn friend
relations.note: He comes at dawn to play counters with Anselm, and he always asks after me first.

memories.gist: The night Anselm carried me up the lamp house stair as a small child, and the light turning above us.
The first winter I rendered oil alone, and burned my wrist on the pan, and told no one for a week.
Lark Morrow at dusk, saying she saw a sail, and the two of us standing on the mole looking at the Pale until the light came on.
A night the oil ran short and Anselm fed the lamp the last measure and sat up with his hand on the glass; I watched him from the stair.
Counting the oil measures against the fish one week and finding the light burned more than I had thought.

stances.why: It is the vow of this house and the work of my days; I would not be the one to let it go out.
I have asked who the light is for and been given only the vow; that is not an answer, and I mean to find one.
She is not a fool and she does not invent things; if she says she saw a sail, she saw something.
The ledger has paid for the oil every year since the Last Sail; that is a debt, not a kindness.
When I cannot settle a question I render another measure and think while the fire does its work.
